title: Claude just found a CRISPR-like DNA pattern, but even Anthropic's scientists aren't sure what it does
key_facts: Late September 2026 Anthropic said Claude found a repeating DNA stretch in a bacteriophage (a virus that infects bacteria).
The repeats sit next to a gene for a reverse transcriptase, an enzyme that copies RNA into DNA, and resemble the repeats in CRISPR.
Anthropic's head of life sciences Eric Kauderer-Abrams says what the system does is still unknown.
Claude was given a fairly generic prompt and found the repeats while looking for accessory proteins.
The related genes seem limited to jumbo phages, which have very large genomes.
Claude did the analysis in about a day; a human scientist would need weeks to months, Anthropic says.
Both scientists stress Claude does not replace biologists and the finding is at the very beginning.
quote_evidence: “What this internal domain does, we’re still not sure,” Kauderer-Abrams adds.
we have no idea what its function is yet, and we’re at the very beginning of the research.
why_it_matters_hint: AI agent found a candidate biological tool in under a day, but its function is unknown.
notes: The discovery was announced by Anthropic in late September; this is the Scientific American interview with two Anthropic scientists. Anthropic's claims, no outside review.
